sentences.i: The rooster said to the dog: and how is that? So the dog told the rooster the whole story again.
sentences.n: أَعَادَ عَلَى, "repeated upon," is simply "recounted to, told again."

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الدِّيكُ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ أُسْتَاذَنَا قَلِيلُ الْعَقْلِ إِنَّ لِي خَمْسِينَ زَوْجَةً أُرَاضِي هَذِهِ وَأُصَالِحُ هَذِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-dīku wa-Allāhi inna ustādhanā qalīlu al-ʿaqli inna lī khamsīna zawjatan urāḍī hādhihi wa-uṣāliḥu hādhihi
sentences.l: So the rooster said: by God, indeed our master is scant of wit — indeed to me are fifty wives; I please this one and I make peace with that one.
sentences.i: The rooster said: by God, our master is a fool. I myself have fifty wives — I keep this one content, and make my peace with that one.
sentences.n: The two إِنَّ-clauses run one after the other with no connective, a brisk feature of this oral style; the second reads as a fresh, emphatic assertion rather than a subordinate one.

sentences.t: وَأُسْتَاذُنَا مَا لَهُ إِلَّا فَرْدُ زَوْجَةٍ وَلَا يَعْرِفُ يَسُوسُ أَمْرَهُ مَعَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ustādhunā mā lahu illā fardu zawjatin wa-lā yaʿrifu yasūsu amrahu maʿahā
sentences.l: While our master — there is not to him except a single wife, and he does not know he manages his affair with her.
sentences.i: While our master has but a single wife, and does not even know how to manage his affair with her.
sentences.n: يَعْرِفُ يَسُوسُ strings two finite verbs together with no linking particle, where Classical prose would insert أَنْ ("know how to manage") — a colloquial complementation pattern worth noting when you meet it again.

sentences.t: مَا لَهُ لَمْ يَأْخُذْ لَهَا مِنْ عِيدَانِ التُّوتِ وَيَدْخُلْ إِلَى خِزَانَةٍ وَيَضْرِبْهَا حَتَّى تَمُوتَ أَوْ تَتُوبَ وَلَا تَعُودَ تَسْأَلُهُ عَنْ شَيْ
sentences.tr: mā lahu lam yaʾkhudh lahā min ʿīdāni al-tūti wa-yadkhul ilā khizānatin wa-yaḍribhā ḥattā tamūta aw tatūba wa-lā taʿūda tasʾaluhu ʿan shay
sentences.l: What is it with him, he does not take for her some of the mulberry rods, and go into a closet, and beat her, until she dies or repents, and does not go back to asking him about anything.
sentences.i: What is wrong with him, that he does not take a few mulberry switches for her, go with her into a closet, and beat her until she either dies or repents, and never goes back to questioning him about anything?
sentences.n: شَيْ is the edition's colloquial spelling of شَيْءٍ, "anything," dropping its final hamza entirely — the same reduced form still heard in spoken Arabic; it is left exactly as printed rather than restored. عِيدَانُ التُّوتِ, "mulberry rods," are switches meant for beating.

sentences.t: قَالَ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التَّاجِرُ كَلَامَ الدِّيكِ وَهُوَ يُخَاطِبُ الْكَلْبَ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā samiʿa al-tājiru kalāma al-dīki wa-huwa yukhāṭibu al-kalba
sentences.l: He said: and when the merchant heard the speech of the rooster, while it was addressing the dog —
sentences.i: He said: now when the merchant heard the rooster's words, as it spoke to the dog —
sentences.n: This قَالَ is the narrator's own voice resuming — a bare "he said" marking a turn in the telling, not a new speaker inside the fable. The clause it opens is completed only in the next unit.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْوَزِيرُ لِابْنَتِهِ شَهْرَزَادَ أَفْعَلُ مَعَكِ مِثْلَ مَا فَعَلَ التَّاجِرُ بِزَوْجَتِهِ
sentences.tr: qāla al-wazīru li-ibnatihi Shahrazāda afʿalu maʿaki mithla mā faʿala al-tājiru bi-zawjatihi
sentences.l: The vizier said to his daughter Shahrazad: I do with you the like of what the merchant did with his wife.
sentences.i: The vizier said to his daughter Shahrazad: I will do to you as the merchant did to his wife.
sentences.n: أَفْعَلُ is first person, "I will do," not the imperative — the vizier is not commanding her but warning her what he himself intends, if she will not be turned aside.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ وَمَا فَعَلَ قَالَ دَخَلَ بِهَا إِلَى الْخِزَانَةِ ثُمَّ بَعْدَ مَا قَطَعَ عَلَيْهَا مِنْ عِيدَانِ التُّوتِ وَخَبَأَهُمْ دَاخِلَ الْخِزَانَةِ دَخَلَ الْخِزَانَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu wa-mā faʿala qāla dakhala bihā ilā al-khizānati thumma baʿda mā qaṭaʿa ʿalayhā min ʿīdāni al-tūti wa-khabaʾahum dākhila al-khizānati dakhala al-khizānata
sentences.l: So she said to him: and what did he do? He said: he entered with her into the closet. Then, after he had cut against her some of the mulberry rods and hidden them inside the closet, he entered the closet.
sentences.i: She said to him: and what did he do? He said: he took her into the closet. Then, after he had cut some mulberry rods for use against her and hidden them inside the closet, he went into the closet.
sentences.n: عَلَيْهَا here is best read as "for use against her" — the rods he cuts are meant for the beating to come, and he prepares and hides them beforehand.

sentences.t: وَقَٰلَ لَهَا تَعَالَى حَتَّى أَقُولَ لَكِ دَاخِلَ الْخِزَانَةِ وَأَمُوتَ وَلَا يَنْظُرَنِي أَحَدٌ فَدَخَلَتْ مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahā taʿālā ḥattā aqūla laki dākhila al-khizānati wa-amūta wa-lā yanẓuranī aḥadun fa-dakhalat maʿahu
sentences.l: And he said to her: come, so that I may tell you, inside the closet, and I may die and let no one see me. So she entered with him.
sentences.i: And he said to her: come, that I may tell you inside the closet, and die there where no one can see me. So she went in with him.
sentences.n: This is his ruse: he frames it as needing privacy to die unseen once he has told her — the very fate the opening premise attached to telling anyone the secret at all. The edition again prints قل for قال here, pointed with the dagger alif as before.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ قَفَلَ بَابَ الْخِزَانَةِ عَلَيْهَا وَنَزَلَ عَلَيْهَا بِالضَّرْبِ إِلَى أَنْ أُغْمِيَ عَلَيْهَا فَقَالَتْ لَهُ تُبْتُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu qafala bāba al-khizānati ʿalayhā wa-nazala ʿalayhā bi-al-ḍarbi ilā an ughmiya ʿalayhā fa-qālat lahu tubtu
sentences.l: Then indeed he locked the door of the closet upon her, and came down upon her with the beating, until she was overcome. So she said to him: I repent.
sentences.i: Then he locked the closet door upon her, and fell upon her with blows, until she swooned. Then she said to him: I repent!
sentences.n: نَزَلَ عَلَيْهَا بِالضَّرْبِ, literally "came down upon her with the beating," is the standing idiom for setting upon someone violently. أُغْمِيَ عَلَيْهَا, passive, "she was overcome," is the ordinary way of saying that someone fainted.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا بَاسَتْ يَدَيْهِ وَرِجْلَيْهِ وَتَابَتْ وَخَرَجَتْ هِيَ وَإِيَّاهُ وَفَرِحُوا الْجَمَاعَةُ وَأَهْلُهَا وَقَعَدُوا فِي أَسَرِّ الْأَحْوَالِ إِلَى الْمَمَاتِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā bāsat yadayhi wa-rijlayhi wa-tābat wa-kharajat hiya wa-iyyāhu wa-fariḥū al-jamāʿatu wa-ahluhā wa-qaʿadū fī asarri al-aḥwāli ilā al-mamāt
sentences.l: Then indeed she kissed his two hands and his two feet, and repented, and went out, she and he together; and the company and her people rejoiced, and they settled into the happiest of states until death.
sentences.i: Then she kissed his hands and his feet, and repented, and the two of them came out together; and the company and her people rejoiced, and they lived on in the happiest of conditions until death.
sentences.n: فِي أَسَرِّ الْأَحْوَالِ, "in the happiest of states," is a fixed idiom of contentment, closing the fable on its own formulaic note, the Arabic equivalent of "and they lived happily ever after."

sentences.t: قَالَ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ ابْنَةُ الْوَزِيرِ مَقَالَةَ أَبِيهَا قَالَتْ لَهُ لَابُدَّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā samiʿati ibnatu al-wazīri maqālata abīhā qālat lahu lā budda min dhālik
sentences.l: He said: and when the vizier's daughter heard her father's speech, she said to him: there is no escape from that.
sentences.i: He said: now when the vizier's daughter heard her father's words, she said to him: there is no help for it.
sentences.n: لَا بُدَّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ, "there is no escape from that," is Shahrazad's flat refusal to be turned aside — the cautionary tale has failed to move her, and the frame story moves on regardless.

sentences.t: فَجَهَّزَهَا وَطَلَعَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ شَهْرِيَارَ
sentences.tr: fa-jahhazahā wa-ṭalaʿa ilā al-maliki Shahriyāra
sentences.l: So he made her ready, and went up to King Shahriyar.
sentences.i: So he made her ready and brought her in to King Shahriyar.
sentences.n: طَلَعَ إِلَى here carries the sense of 'went in to (a person)', much as دَخَلَ عَلَى does elsewhere in this text. The subject is Shahrazad's father the vizier, and 'her' is Shahrazad herself, about to be given to the king.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ قَدْ أَوْصَتْ أُخْتَهَا الصَّغِيرَةَ وَقَالَتْ لَهَا إِذَا تَوَجَّهْتُ عِنْدَ الْمَلِكِ أُرْسِلُ أَطْلُبُكِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat qad awṣat ukhtahā al-ṣaghīrata wa-qālat lahā idhā tawajjahtu ʿinda al-maliki ursilu aṭlubuki
sentences.l: And she had instructed her younger sister, and said to her: ‘When I have gone to the king, I send — I summon you.’
sentences.i: Now she had already charged her younger sister beforehand, telling her: ‘When I am taken in to the king, I will send for you.’
sentences.n: كَانَتْ قَدْ أَوْصَتْ is a pluperfect, marking a flashback: the story steps back to explain an arrangement made before Shahrazad ever entered the king's chamber. The speaker is Shahrazad; أُرْسِلُ أَطْلُبُكِ strings two first-person verbs together with no conjunction — literally 'I send, I summon you' — the ordinary way this prose says 'I will send for you.'

sentences.t: فَإِذَا جِئْتِ إِلَى عِنْدِي وَرَأَيْتِ الْمَلِكَ قَضَى حَاجَتَهُ مِنِّي تَقُولِي يَا أُخْتِي حَدِّثِينِي حَدِيثًا وَكَلَامًا نَقْطَعُ بِهِ اللَّيْلَ وَالسَّهَرَ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā jiʾti ilā ʿindī wa-raʾayti al-malika qaḍā ḥājatahu minnī taqūlī yā ukhtī ḥaddithīnī ḥadīthan wa-kalāman naqṭaʿu bihi al-layla wa-al-sahara
sentences.l: Then if you come to me, and you see the king has finished his need of me, you say: ‘O my sister, tell me a story and talk, that we may cut off by it the night and the wakefulness.’
sentences.i: Then, once you have come to me and seen that the king has had his will of me, say: ‘O my sister, tell me some tale or discourse, that we may while away the night and its sleeplessness.’
sentences.n: قَضَى حَاجَتَهُ مِنِّي, 'he finished his need of me', is the Arabic's own euphemism for the consummation of the marriage; the translation keeps it exactly as indirect as the original. تَقُولِي, without its final nūn, functions here as the command that answers the conditional — 'you are to say' — not a plain statement of fact.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أُحَدِّثُكِ حَدِيثًا يَكُونُ فِيهِ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى الْخَلَاصُ
sentences.tr: wa-anā uḥaddithuki ḥadīthan yakūnu fīhi in shāʾa Allāhu taʿālā al-khalāṣu
sentences.l: And I — I will tell you a story in which will be, God willing, the deliverance.
sentences.i: And I shall tell you a tale in which, God willing, our deliverance will lie.
sentences.n: يَكُونُ فِيهِ ... الْخَلَاصُ inverts the usual word order (predicate before subject) for emphasis: literally 'in it will be — the deliverance'. The line states outright, this early, what the whole frame story is building toward.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ أَبَاهَا الْوَزِيرَ طَلَعَ بِهَا إِلَى الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna abāhā al-wazīra ṭalaʿa bihā ilā al-maliki
sentences.l: Then indeed her father the vizier went up with her to the king.
sentences.i: Then her father the vizier brought her in to the king.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُ فَرِحَ وَقَٰلَ أَتَيْتَ بِحَاجَتِي فَقَالَ نَعَمْ وَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَدْخُلَ عَلَيْهَا فَبَكَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu fariḥa wa-qāla atayta bi-ḥājatī fa-qāla naʿam wa-arāda an yadkhula ʿalayhā fa-bakat
sentences.l: And when he saw him, he rejoiced, and said: ‘You have brought my need.’ And he said: ‘Yes.’ And he wished to go in to her, and she wept.
sentences.i: When he saw him he rejoiced, and said, ‘Have you brought me what I wanted?’ ‘Yes,’ he answered. And he made to go in to her — and she wept.
sentences.n: 'He' and 'him' are the king and the vizier. رَآهُ is spelled bare in the edition, راه, so the hamza is supplied here as a combining mark over the alif rather than the precomposed آ used for the same word earlier in the frame story. وَقَٰلَ is likewise the edition's defective spelling قل for قَالَ, pointed with a dagger alif as before. أَتَيْتَ بِحَاجَتِي carries no interrogative particle, but the reply نَعَمْ shows it is meant as a question. يَدْخُلَ عَلَيْهَا, 'to go in to her', is the same euphemism for consummation met above.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا مَالَكِ فَقَالَتْ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ إِنَّ لِي أُخْتًا صَغِيرَةً وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ أُوَدِّعَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā mā laki fa-qālat ayyuhā al-maliku inna lī ukhtan ṣaghīratan wa-urīdu an uwaddiʿahā
sentences.l: So he said to her: ‘What is with you?’ So she said: ‘O King, indeed I have a young sister, and I want that I bid her farewell.’
sentences.i: So he said to her, ‘What ails you?’ And she said, ‘O King, I have a young sister, and I wish to take my leave of her.’
sentences.n: This is the first move of the very stratagem Shahrazad laid out to her sister above: asking to see her once more is how she gets her into the room.

sentences.t: فَأَرْسَلَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَيْهَا فَجَاءَتْ إِلَى أُخْتِهَا وَعَانَقَتْهَا وَجَلَسَتْ تَحْتَ السَّرِيرِ فَقَامَ الْمَلِكُ وَأَخَذَ بَكَارَتَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-arsala al-maliku ilayhā fa-jāʾat ilā ukhtihā wa-ʿānaqathā wa-jalasat taḥta al-sarīri fa-qāma al-maliku wa-akhadha bakāratahā
sentences.l: So the king sent for her, and she came to her sister and embraced her, and sat beneath the bed. Then the king arose and took her virginity.
sentences.i: So the king sent for her; and she came in to her sister and embraced her, and sat down beneath the bed. Then the king arose and took her maidenhead.
sentences.n: The pronouns need untangling: the king sends for Dunyazad, the younger sister; she comes in to Shahrazad, embraces her, and hides beneath the bed exactly as arranged, so that once the king is done she can raise the request for a story. بَكَارَتَهَا, 'her virginity', is Shahrazad's; the sentence is as plain in the Arabic as it is kept here.

sentences.t: وَجَلَسُوا يَتَحَدَّثُونَ فَقَالَتْ لَهَا أُخْتُهَا الصَّغِيرَةُ بِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكِ يَا أُخْتِي حَدِّثِينَا حَدِيثًا نَقْطَعُ بِهِ سَهَرَ لَيْلَتِنَا
sentences.tr: wa-jalasū yataḥaddathūna fa-qālat lahā ukhtuhā al-ṣaghīratu bi-llāhi ʿalayki yā ukhtī ḥaddithīnā ḥadīthan naqṭaʿu bihi sahara laylatinā
sentences.l: And they sat conversing. So her younger sister said to her: ‘By God upon you, O my sister, tell us a story, that we may cut off by it the wakefulness of our night.’
sentences.i: And the three of them sat talking; and her younger sister said to her: ‘I adjure you by God, O my sister, tell us a tale, that we may while away the wakefulness of our night.’
sentences.n: بِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكِ is a fixed formula of urgent entreaty, 'I beg you by God', not a literal oath sworn about the person addressed. This request is the hinge the whole book turns on: it is what lets Shahrazad begin telling stories at all.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ حُبًّا وَ كَرَامَةً إِنْ أَذِنَ لِي الْمَلِكُ الْمُهَذَّبُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat ḥubban wa-karāmatan in adhina lī al-maliku al-muhadhdhabu
sentences.l: So she said: ‘Lovingly and honorably — if the courteous king permits me.’
sentences.i: And she said, ‘Gladly, and with all my heart — if the gracious King will give me leave.’
sentences.n: حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً, literally 'with love and with honor', is a set doublet still current today for a willing 'gladly, of course' — not two separate feelings but a single idiom.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ مِنْهُمَا ذَلِكَ وَكَانَ قَلِقًا فَرِحَ لِسَمَاعِ الْحَدِيثِ فَأَذِنَ لَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku minhumā dhālika wa-kāna qaliqan fariḥa li-samāʿi al-ḥadīthi fa-adhina lahā
sentences.l: And when the king heard that from the two of them — and he had been restless — he rejoiced at the hearing of the story, and he permitted her.
sentences.i: And when the king heard this from the two of them — for he had been sleepless himself — he was glad at the thought of a tale to hear, and gave her leave.
sentences.n: وَكَانَ قَلِقًا is a parenthetical aside explaining his gladness: he too had been lying awake, so a story is welcome for his own sake, not merely granted as a favor.

sentences.t: حِكَايَةُ التَّاجِرِ وَالْجِنِّيِّ
sentences.tr: ḥikāyatu al-tājiri wa-al-jinniyyi
sentences.l: The Tale of the Merchant and the Jinni.
sentences.n: This heading marks the start of the first tale Shahrazad tells — the story-within-the-story this whole frame has been building toward.
